title: Soil survey

definition.text: The process of classifying the soil types and other soil properties of an area and recording them geographically; also called soil mapping.

facts.text: Soil surveys apply soil science and draw heavily on geomorphology, theories of soil formation, physical geography and patterns of vegetation and land use.
Primary data come from field sampling and remote sensing, mainly aerial photography, with LiDAR and other digital techniques steadily gaining ground.
Surveyors once carried paper air photos, topographic maps and mapping keys; many now carry a rugged tablet with GPS, digital imagery, LiDAR and soil geodatabases.
In the United States the National Cooperative Soil Survey once published surveys as books for each county; paper surveys could take years to publish.
Surveys are now published on the web through the NRCS Web Soil Survey, where users build custom surveys and changes go live in moments.
A county survey typically holds a general soil map, a detailed map of indexed soil series, a section on soil use and management, and tables of land-use suitability.
NRCS has soil maps and data online for more than 95 percent of US counties.
In the second half of the 20th century soil mapping meant field survey and drawing soil-type boundaries on maps at scales that varied by country and purpose.

notes: Web Soil Survey (a product without its own article) is folded in here and under SSURGO.

title: Soil survey interpretation

definition.text: The use of soil survey information to predict the potentials and limitations of soils for particular uses, such as crops, building or gardens.

facts.text: Farmers and ranchers use it to judge whether a soil suits crops or livestock and what management it needs; architects and engineers use soil engineering properties to judge sites for construction.
Survey data must be interpreted before planners can use them, and the resulting predictions guide land use and management on areas from small tracts to several million acres.
These predictions must be weighed with economic, social and environmental considerations before they become valid land-use recommendations.
Published US surveys include land-use suitability tables based on Natural Resources Conservation Service standards.

notes: Closest material to 'land evaluation', which has no crawled page (see gaps).

definition.text: A geographical representation of the soil types, or of soil properties such as pH, texture, organic matter or horizon depth, across an area.

facts.text: A soil map is usually the product of a soil survey, and traditional maps show only the general distribution of soils alongside the survey report.
Soil maps are used mostly for land evaluation, spatial planning, agricultural extension and environmental protection.
Many new maps come from digital soil mapping; they show more detail but are not necessarily more accurate, and statistical maps can include an estimate of model uncertainty.
Map types include hand-drawn polygon maps of soil types, predicted or simulated 2D or 3D soil-property maps, and predicted soil-class maps.
Maps of primary attributes show what was described or measured in the field; maps of secondary, inferred attributes show properties for a use, such as production capacity or degradation.
Farmers in precision agriculture use soil maps to adjust field inputs.

title: Soil information system

definition.text: A systematic, consistent collection of gridded or vector soil property and class maps, with attached report, manual or metadata, covering a whole area of interest.

facts.text: Digital soil maps are visualisations of soil inventories stored in a soil information system, whose major part is a soil geographical database.
Most combine polygon and point maps linked to attribute tables for profile observations, soil mapping units and soil classes.
ISRIC works to strengthen national, regional and continental soil information systems, and a new global system is being developed under the Global Soil Partnership.

related: International Soil Reference and Information Centre
notes: No article of its own; described on Soil map and mentioned on International Soil Reference and Information Centre and Soil governance.

definition.text: The Soil Survey Geographic database, digital soil data produced and distributed in the United States by the Natural Resources Conservation Service.

facts.text: It records soil types and their distribution, soil characteristics and properties, and the limits, risks and suitability of soils for various uses.
It is the dataset in which the NRCS maintains its soil information.
Its survey data reach users through Web Soil Survey, which the NRCS runs as the single authoritative source of US soil survey information.

definition.text: Germany's comparative rating of soil quality (Bodenwertzahl), scored from soil sampling data on a scale from 0 (very low) to 100 (very high).

facts.text: For arable land it combines field assessments of soil type, soil development and parent material, and expresses the relative net income the soil alone would yield under proper management.
Heavy to clayey loams score 31–50, loams partly covered with loess 51–70 and loams with a loess cover 71–90.
Adjusting the soil value for terrain, climate and location gives the field value, or Ackerzahl.

It began with the Reich Soil Assessment under the 1934 Soil Assessment Act, which set a Magdeburg Börde farm at 100 as the basis for farm tax ratings; a record 102.8 was later measured near Hildesheim.

title: Prime farmland

definition.text: A US Department of Agriculture designation for land with the best combination of physical and chemical characteristics for producing food, feed, forage, fibre and oilseed crops, and available for those uses.

facts.text: Prime farmland has the soil quality, growing season and moisture supply to give economically sustained high yields under acceptable farming methods, including water management.
It generally has a dependable water supply, a favourable temperature and growing season, acceptable acidity or alkalinity, acceptable salt and sodium content, and few or no rocks.
It is not excessively erodible or long saturated with water, and either rarely floods or is protected from flooding.

Because many cities grew up in rich farming areas, prime farmland is also well suited to housing, and the designation helps growth management use zoning, conservation easements and green belts to keep it.

Complementary USDA designations are farmland of statewide importance, farmland of local importance and unique farmland, the last used for specific high-value crops such as nuts, olives, cranberries and citrus.
State and local agencies set the criteria for the statewide and local categories in cooperation with the USDA.
Preserving prime farmland soils is hard when they occupy less than 60% of an area, so a universal demarcation method joining science and policy is needed.

notes: Land-conversion sentence S:620ac4913210 carries CITATION NEEDED and was not used.

definition.text: The computer-assisted production of digital maps of soil types and soil properties, also called predictive soil mapping.

facts.text: The Working Group on Digital Soil Mapping defines it as building geographically referenced soil databases at a set resolution from field and laboratory observations linked to environmental data by quantitative relationships.
It is distinct from traditional soil mapping, in which field soil scientists draw soil boundaries by hand, though hand-drawn maps can also be digitised.
It relies on GPS, field scanners and remote sensing, together with geostatistical interpolation, GIS, digital elevation models and data mining.
Semi-automated methods lower costs, and its products are routinely assessed for accuracy and uncertainty and are easier to update as new data arrive.
It tries to overcome traditional maps that often only delineate soil classes, give no basis for modelling changing soil conditions and are inflexible for quantitative studies of soil function.
Examples include EU maps of texture and bulk density from about 20,000 LUCAS topsoil samples, and ISRIC's global SoilGrids maps at 250 m resolution built with machine learning.

definition.text: Data-driven production of soil property and soil class maps by statistical methods, also called statistical soil mapping.

facts.text: It predicts soil variables at unsampled places and estimates the uncertainty of each prediction by statistical inference, largely through geostatistics.
Its practical aim is to predict how a soil-plant ecosystem will respond to management, producing maps for environmental models and decisions.
Traditional survey infers soil bodies from mental models and draws them by hand, which is subjective and hard to test for accuracy without extra sampling.
Pedometric outputs come from rigorous statistical computing, so they are reproducible.
It leans on detailed covariate layers such as elevation-model derivatives, remote sensing imagery and climate, land cover and geology data.
Traditional mapping targets soil types as discrete bodies on polygon maps; pedometric mapping targets measured properties as continuous grids with prediction-error maps.
Unlike digital soil mapping, it relies strictly on geostatistics and does not delineate discrete soil types.
Its workflow runs from data screening and covariate preparation through model fitting, spatial prediction and cross-validation to visualisation.

definition.text: The application of mathematical and statistical methods to the study of the distribution and genesis of soils.

facts.text: The name joins the Greek pedos, 'soil', and metron, 'measurement'.
It tackles soil problems clouded by deterministic or random variation, vagueness and lack of knowledge, using simulation models built on chaos theory, statistical distributions or fuzzy logic.
It is a sub-discipline of pedology focused on quantitative techniques, especially for mapping soil properties.
Its advance is tied to better remote and close-range sensing and to wavelets, fuzzy sets and data mining.

definition.text: A model that splits a soil variable at any place into a deterministic trend, a spatially autocorrelated random part and leftover noise: Z(s) = m(s) + ε′(s) + ε″.

facts.text: French mathematician Georges Matheron introduced it, and it has proven the best unbiased linear predictor for spatial data.
Regression-kriging, also called universal kriging, uses it to make soil predictions or simulations.
For soils the deterministic part is often modelled from Hans Jenny's soil-forming factors of climate, organisms, relief, parent material and time, the CLORPT model.

definition.text: A soil rating method based on the soil characteristics that govern a land's potential use and productive capacity.

facts.text: R. Earl Storie developed it at the University of California, Berkeley, in the 1930s for land valuation, independent of other physical or economic factors.
It rates soil depth and texture, permeability, chemical characteristics, drainage and runoff, and climate where climate is not uniform.
The index multiplies these ratings, so a zero in any one makes the whole result zero.
Its ratings are subjective; O'Geen and colleagues updated the method in 2008 to reduce this.

title: European Soil Database

definition.text: The only harmonized soil database in Europe, the source of many other soil data, information and services.

facts.text: Its v2 Raster Library holds public-domain grids with 1 km x 1 km cells, aligned with the INSPIRE reference grid, for many soil parameters.
Parameters include texture, parent material, WRB soil type, soil depth, mineralogy, cation exchange capacity and available water capacity.
It is based on experts' knowledge, and the European Commission's LUCAS topsoil survey adds sampled soil data across the European Union.
Combined with land cover, climate and topography data, it gives the most homogeneous data on the organic carbon content of European soils.

related: World Reference Base for Soil Resources
notes: A regional data resource; kept because it has its own article (test 1). Kind set to Method for want of a data-resource kind.

definition.text: Taking photographs of landscapes and surface features from aircraft or other airborne platforms.

facts.text: Vertical aerial photographs underpin photogrammetric surveys, the usual basis of topographic maps, and are used in land-use planning.
Photogrammetry, mapping from aerial photographs, was pioneered commercially in the 1930s.
One of Fairchild's first government contracts was an aerial survey of New Mexico to study soil erosion.
Stereoscopic pairs of aerial photographs have often been used by terrain analysts to make topographic maps.

definition.text: Gathering information about an object or area from a distance, usually with sensors on satellites or aircraft, instead of measuring it on site.

facts.text: It is active when the sensor emits a signal and detects its reflection, and passive when it detects reflected sunlight.
Soil moisture, surface water storage, precipitation and evapotranspiration can all be measured by remote sensing at various resolutions and accuracies.
Land cover and land use maps from thematic mapping can detect deforestation and track the health of crops and native plants.
Agricultural and environmental statistics usually combine classified satellite images with ground-truth data from a field sample.
Interferometric synthetic aperture radar produces precise digital elevation models of large areas of terrain.

definition.text: A computer representation of elevation data that depicts terrain, or the objects on top of it.

facts.text: A digital terrain model shows the bare ground surface, while a digital surface model may include tree canopy and buildings; the terms are not used consistently.
DEMs are usually built from remote sensing, such as photogrammetry, lidar or radar interferometry, but can also come from land surveying.
Terrain models are needed for drainage modelling and land-use studies, and DEMs are widely used in geographic information systems.
Uses include extracting terrain parameters for geomorphology and modelling soil wetness with depth-to-water indexes.

definition.text: Integrated computer hardware and software that store, manage, analyse, edit and display geographic data.

facts.text: A GIS relates otherwise unrelated information by using location as the key index variable.
The first, the Canada Geographic Information System, handled the Canada Land Inventory, which mapped soils, agriculture, forestry and land use at 1:50,000 to judge rural land capability.
GIS data typically represent features such as roads, land use, elevation and waterways; masses such as the soil types of an area are represented less directly.
Survey data can be entered directly into a GIS from digital survey instruments by coordinate geometry.

definition.text: An FAO method of land evaluation that appraises and groups areas of land by their fitness for a defined use.

facts.text: Land can be assessed in its present condition or after improvements.
It has four categories of decreasing generality: orders (kinds of suitability), classes (degrees), subclasses (kinds of limitation) and units (minor management differences).
There are two orders: S, land whose sustained use yields benefits justifying the inputs without unacceptable damage, and N, land whose qualities seem to rule that use out.
Land may be Not Suitable because the use is impracticable, would cause severe degradation such as cultivating steep slopes, or, most often, would not repay its costs.
Climate change shifts land suitability for many crops, usually toward higher latitudes and altitudes.

definition.text: The numbered degrees of suitability within each FAO land suitability order, in decreasing order of suitability.

facts.text: The number of Suitable classes is not fixed but should be kept minimal, probably never more than five.
With three Suitable classes, S1 is highly suitable, S2 moderately suitable and S3 marginally suitable, the last only marginally justifying the inputs.
Not Suitable land normally has two classes: N1, limitations that might be overcome in time but not at acceptable cost now, and N2, limitations ruling out any sustained use.

definition.text: A map showing the potential uses, usually for farming, of each unit of land.

facts.text: The commonest indicators are five physical factors: rock type, soil type, slope, erosion degree and type, and vegetation.
It differs from a land use map, which shows how land is actually used now.
In the United States the Soil Conservation Service developed the Land Capability System in 1951, and soil survey standards keep data consistent with it.

definition.text: An online service run by the USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service that gives access to soil data from the National Cooperative Soil Survey.

facts.text: US soil surveys are no longer printed as books; they are published on Web Soil Survey, where users can build a custom soil survey.
It holds everything in the old county reports plus extra tools, and can be updated as needed, whereas new surveys of the same county took 30 to 60 years.
A user picks an area of interest anywhere in the United States where survey data exist; the Soil Map tab then shows the area's component soil map units, and a report can be saved as a PDF.
The Soil Data Explorer gives properties for each map unit, such as depth to water table, surface texture, bulk density, pH and depth to a restrictive layer, along with suitability ratings for uses.
Ratings cover uses such as dwellings with basements, local roads and streets, vegetative productivity and wastewater disposal by irrigation, each with reasons for the rating.
It is one recognized basis, alongside measured infiltration rates, for choosing the hydrologic soil group of a site.

definition.text: A forestry measure of a site's potential for tree growth, given as the height of dominant and co-dominant trees at a base age.

facts.text: Base ages such as 25, 50 and 100 years are used; a 50-year-old red oak 70 feet (21 m) tall gives a site index of 70.
Site index is specific to each tree species.
It can be found from tree height, from understory indicator plants, or from soil maps.
In the United States the NRCS measured site index on surveyed soils and tabulated soils against site indexes for important species.
Indirect estimates use dominant species, lesser vegetation, and topographic, climatic and edaphic factors.
Despite shortcomings, it has been the most widely used way of estimating site productivity in North America.

definition.text: Graphs or equations that convert a stand's measured dominant height and age into its site index.

facts.text: Height comes from a dominant or co-dominant site tree measured with a clinometer, laser hypsometer or releskop; age from an increment borer or planting records.
On a curve, a 60-foot (18 m) tree in a 50-year-old stand is read where age 50 on the x-axis meets 60 feet on the y-axis; the nearest line gives the site index.
One equation is lnS = lnHd − b1(A⁻¹ − Ai⁻¹), where S is site index, Hd dominant height, A stand age and Ai index age.
For planted white spruce, curves cannot be reliably extended below about 15 years because early growth is hard to predict.

definition.text: A small-scale soil survey of low-value land that identifies regions dominated by soil associations rather than delineating individual soils.

facts.text: Large expanses of land with little direct agricultural or forest value are often too poor to justify the cost of a detailed survey, so they are mapped at small scale.
A reconnaissance survey shows soil associations, in contrast to the detailed map in which specific soils are delineated.

title: Soil association

definition.text: A general pattern of several main soils that repeats across a landscape, shown on a general soil map.

facts.text: After studying the soils of an area, surveyors can make a general map showing the main patterns of soils, called soil associations.
Each association has a few major soils and several minor soils in a characteristic, though not strictly uniform, pattern.

notes: Article null: concept appears on the survey page only; passes test 6 (curated lab manual teaches it as a map type).

definition.text: A subdivision of a soil series made when slope, erosion, stoniness or another feature changes how the soil can be used.

facts.text: Series vary so much in slope, erosion, stones or similar features that management advice could not be given if each were shown as one unit, so they are divided into soil phases.
The phase name gives the surface feature that most affects management; Vina loam 0 to 2 percent slopes and Vina gravelly loam 2 to 9 percent slopes are two of four phases of the Vina series.
The area inside each continuous line on a soil map is the delineation of a map unit.
A map unit includes the soil phase and all inclusions.

definition.text: A description of what people do on a parcel of land, covering the benefits taken from it and the management actions applied.

facts.text: The IPCC groups land use into forest land, cropland, grassland, wetlands, settlements and other lands, and defines it as the total of arrangements, activities and inputs applied to a parcel.
The FAO defines land use as the products and benefits obtained from land together with the management actions people carry out to obtain them.
Land use and management practices strongly affect water, soil, nutrients, plants and animals; poor choices contribute to soil erosion, soil degradation, land degradation and desertification.
Arable land was about 10.7% of the land surface in 2015, with 1.3% permanent cropland; early-1990s figures were 13% arable, 26% pasture and 32% forest and woodland.
Governments plan and regulate land use through zoning and other ordinances to avoid land-use conflicts; an urban growth boundary is one such tool.

definition.text: The change from one land-use category to another, mostly driven by human activity.

facts.text: Land-use change and fossil fuel use are the major human sources of carbon dioxide, a dominant greenhouse gas.
Deforestation, the permanent conversion of forest to other uses, has historically been a primary driver, and global forest cover has fallen by 35% since agriculture began.
Urban areas cover just 3% of the Earth's surface, yet their growth shifts demand onto rural land and can take over adjacent cropland.
Scientists track land change with satellite imagery, aircraft imagery, field observations and modelling, and use land change models to simulate possible futures for planning.
